sysd-msg-101.title: Polling: asking again and again whether anything is new
sysd-msg-101.text: Polling is like constantly asking whether there is anything new, even when there may be no update. It means repeatedly checking an external device or service for its status, a synchronous activity driven by the client, to retrieve updated information. That makes it resource-intensive and inefficient. The client gets updates only when it asks, so it can miss real-time information, though developers gain more control over when and how data is fetched. With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data. It is a solid option when an infrastructure limitation prevents the use of {{ref:sysd-msg-102}}. Polling fails to scale when there are too many devices to check, because the time needed to poll them can exceed the time available to service them. The alternative is interrupts, signals from devices that say they need attention. In many situations they cut processor spinning and bandwidth use.

sysd-msg-098.title: Push technology: the server speaks first
sysd-msg-098.text: In push technology, also called server push, the server rather than the client starts the exchange. That differs from the pull method, where the client initiates it. Clients usually say which information they want through the publish-subscribe model. A client subscribes to channels on a server, and the server pushes new content to subscribed clients automatically. Chat and synchronous conferencing are push services, because messages are pushed to the user as soon as the messaging service receives them. Push-enabled web applications include software updates, stock tickers, webchat, auctions, online betting and gaming, and sport results. Email is only partly push. SMTP is a push protocol. But the last step, from mail server to desktop, usually uses a pull protocol such as POP3 or IMAP, which clients poll frequently. IMAP's IDLE command lets the server tell the client when new messages arrive. Push is not always available. When restrictive security policies block incoming HTTP requests, push is sometimes simulated by polling, in which the client periodically checks the server for new information.

sysd-msg-100.title: Long polling: holding the request open until there is news
sysd-msg-100.text: A server that is asked whether anything is new can decline to answer until there is. That is long polling. If the server has nothing new when the poll arrives, it holds the request open instead of sending an empty response. It replies only when information is available or a timeout threshold is reached. The reply completes the open request, and the client immediately, or after a defined interval, issues another to re-establish a pending connection. Unlike normal polling, this removes the response latency between information becoming available and the client's next request. It is not true push, though. It emulates server push where real push is not possible, such as sites whose security policies reject incoming HTTP requests. It is easy to implement, nearly universally supported and good for small-scale projects. But it is usually not scalable, because every response needs a new connection, which is intensive on the server. Reliable message ordering can also be an issue across multiple requests.

sysd-msg-105.title: Push notification: a message from the server to your screen
sysd-msg-105.text: A push notification can show a short message, set a badge on the app icon, light the notification LED or play an alert sound. It is a message pushed from a back-end server or application to a user interface such as a mobile or desktop application. Typical content is chat messages, vendor special offers, event reminders and changes to subscribed topics such as the weather. Notifications are either local or remote. For a local one, the application schedules the notification with the device's OS. For a remote one, a server sends it. The client application registers on the server with a unique key, such as a UUID or Apple Device Token. The server then sends the message against that key over a protocol such as HTTP or {{ref:sysd-msg-148}}. Real-time push notifications can raise privacy issues, since they can be used to link social network pseudonyms to the real identities of smartphone owners.

sysd-msg-107.title: Web push: one connection for every event
sysd-msg-107.text: Radio use is a major drain on mobile devices, and separate persistent connections, each with its keep-alive traffic, waste it. Web push consolidates all events into one session through a single service that distributes them as they arrive. It is the set of web standards that deliver real-time events such as incoming calls or messages to a user, based on a simple protocol over HTTP/2. The model has three actors: a user agent, a push service and an application server. A subscription is two resources. A private subscription resource lets the user agent receive messages and delete the subscription. A public push resource is shared with the application server to send messages. The user agent POSTs to the push service to subscribe and gets 201 Created. The application server POSTs the message body to the push resource. For at-least-once delivery, the user agent must acknowledge each message with an HTTP DELETE. Chrome, Firefox and Edge implement the W3C Push API fully, and Safari partly, as of February 2023.

sysd-msg-099.title: Techniques for real-time updates over HTTP
sysd-msg-099.text: An HTTP server cannot automatically initiate a connection to a browser, so the browser has to start things. Web applications were built around a client-server model in which the client always starts a transaction. That left the server no way to push data without first receiving a request. Two families of technique work around it. In the first, the browser does the heavy lifting by polling. With short polling the browser keeps retrying until it gets the latest data. With long polling the server does not return a result until new data has arrived. In the second, the browser and server cooperate through {{ref:sysd-msg-108}} or {{ref:sysd-msg-103}}. Once the connection is established, the server can send the latest data straight to the browser. The two differ in direction. SSE is uni-directional, so the browser cannot send a new request to the server, while its rival is full-duplex, so the browser can keep sending new requests.

sysd-msg-108.title: WebSocket: one persistent channel, open both ways
sysd-msg-108.text:
Before WebSocket, a two-way web app had to fake it. It polled over several HTTP connections and sent upstream messages as separate calls. That meant multiple TCP connections per client, an HTTP header on every message and client-side tracking of replies. WebSocket is a communications protocol that gives a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection. The channel is persistent, so client and server can each send data at any time, independently of the other.

That gives full-duplex interaction with lower overhead than half-duplex alternatives such as HTTP polling, because the server can send content without being asked first. RFC 6455 describes an independent TCP-based protocol: a thin layer that adds an origin-based security model, naming, framing and a closing handshake. HTTP servers see only its handshake, as an Upgrade request. TCP alone deals with streams of bytes with no inherent notion of a message. WebSocket enables streams of messages on top of it.

It suits games, stock tickers, multiuser applications with simultaneous editing, and user interfaces that expose server-side services in real time. Its advantages are full-duplex asynchronous messaging, a better origin-based security model, and light weight for both client and server. Its limits are that terminated connections are not automatically recovered and older browsers lack support, though modern major browsers support the standardized protocol.

sysd-msg-109.title: WebSocket opening handshake: an HTTP request that switches protocols
sysd-msg-109.text:
A WebSocket begins life as an ordinary HTTP request. The client sends a GET Upgrade request, with HTTP version at least 1.1, so one port can serve both HTTP clients and WebSocket clients. The request carries Host, Upgrade: websocket, Connection: Upgrade, a Sec-WebSocket-Key of 16 random bytes base64-encoded, Sec-WebSocket-Version 13, and an Origin header from browser clients.

The server must prove it received the handshake, so that it does not accept connections that are not WebSocket connections, such as crafted XMLHttpRequest or form submissions. To prove it, the server appends a fixed GUID to the Sec-WebSocket-Key value, takes the SHA-1 hash, base64-encodes it and returns it in Sec-WebSocket-Accept. Another source says these headers are meant to stop a caching proxy from re-sending a previous WebSocket conversation. It adds that they give no way to check who is connecting, no privacy and no integrity.

The server then replies 101 (Switching Protocols). Any other status means the handshake has not completed and HTTP semantics still apply. The client sends no frames if the Sec-WebSocket-Accept value is missing or wrong. A server that rejects the handshake must return an HTTP error. Examples are 403 Forbidden for an unwanted origin, 426 Upgrade Required, with its supported versions, for a wrong version, and 404 Not Found for an unavailable service. After the 101 response HTTP is no longer used, and both sides can send data in either direction over a binary frame-based protocol. A WebSocket can also be established over HTTP/2 with the extended CONNECT method of RFC 8441. That carries it in one stream, so other streams keep carrying HTTP traffic. RFC 9220 adapts this for HTTP/3.

sysd-msg-110.title: WebSocket frames and messages
sysd-msg-110.text: After the opening handshake, either side may send data messages (text or binary) and control messages (Close, Ping, Pong) at any time. The protocol is frame-based rather than stream-based, with minimal framing. A message is one frame if unfragmented and two or more if fragmented. Intermediaries may split or coalesce frames, so endpoints must not depend on frame boundaries. Fragmentation lets a sender start a message of unknown length without buffering it. Fragments must arrive in order and must not interleave with another message's fragments unless an extension allows it. Control frames may be injected between fragments, so a ping is not stuck behind a large message, but they are never fragmented. A frame header holds a FIN bit, set on the last frame of a message, and three reserved bits. It also holds a 4-bit opcode, a mask bit, a payload length and, if the mask bit is 1, a 32-bit masking key. Opcodes are 0 continuation, 1 text, 2 binary, 8 Close, 9 Ping and 10 Pong.

sysd-msg-115.title: WebSocket through proxies and load balancers
sysd-msg-115.text: WebSocket is unaware of proxies and firewalls, yet its handshake is HTTP-compatible, so it can pass through HTTP infrastructure. HTTP servers can share ports 80 and 443 with a WebSocket gateway or server. Behind a configured proxy, the client sets up a persistent tunnel with HTTP CONNECT. Some proxies are transparent and work with WebSocket. Others make the connection fail, and unencrypted traffic through a proxy without WebSocket support will likely fail. Encrypted WebSocket Secure connections succeed more often, and connections on port 443 are significantly more likely to succeed than on port 80. Load balancers add their own demands. They must support persistent connections, so a server can keep a WebSocket open with a client. Dedicated hosts for WebSocket connections, separate from the HTTP servers, are probably easier to manage. Interactive messaging traffic can induce unusual loads on some components. Nginx has acted as reverse proxy and load balancer for WebSocket applications since 2013.

sysd-msg-113.title: WebSocket closing handshake: ending a connection cleanly
sysd-msg-113.text:
A WebSocket ends with a polite exchange. Either peer can start by sending a Close control frame, opcode 8. The other replies with a Close frame if it has not already sent one, and both peers may safely start it at the same time. After sending a Close frame a peer sends no more data frames, and after receiving one it discards further data. Once an endpoint has both sent and received Close, it must close the TCP connection. The server does so immediately, and the client ideally waits for the server to do it.

It complements the TCP closing handshake, which is not always reliable end to end with intercepting proxies. It also avoids cases where data is lost unnecessarily. Servers may close the connection whenever they want, but clients should not close it arbitrarily. Either way, closure begins with the closing handshake.

A Close frame may carry a 2-byte status code followed by a UTF-8 reason of at most 123 bytes, which clients must not show to end users. Defined codes include 1000 normal closure, 1001 going away, 1002 protocol error and 1003 unsupported data. Others are 1007 invalid payload data, 1008 policy violated, 1009 message too big and 1011 internal server error. Codes 1005, 1006 and 1015 are reserved and must not be sent in a Close frame. The range 1000 to 2999 belongs to the protocol, 3000 to 3999 to libraries and frameworks registered with IANA, and 4000 to 4999 to private use.

sysd-msg-106.title: Notification system architecture: from business service to your inbox
sysd-msg-106.text: A notification system takes notifications from business services, validates and schedules them, and delivers them through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes. It covers in-app notifications, email notifications, SMS and OTP notifications, and social media pushes. The path has stages. Business services send notifications to a notification gateway, which can take one at a time or batches of them. The gateway forwards them to a distribution service that validates, formats and schedules them according to settings. Two repositories feed it: a template repository pre-defines message formats, and a channel preference repository pre-defines preferred delivery channels. Notifications then go to routers, normally message queues, and channel services pass them to the internal and external delivery channels. Last, a tracking and analytics service captures delivery metrics, so the operations team can view reports and improve the user experience.

sysd-msg-102.title: Webhooks: letting the other service call you
sysd-msg-102.text: Why keep asking when the other service can simply tell you? Instead of continuously asking a payment processor or a shipping vendor for information, you create an endpoint in your application server and give it as a callback. That endpoint is a webhook. Every time something interesting happens, the external service calls it and provides the information. Data is pushed to the application as soon as it is available, which makes webhooks ideal for real-time updates. Because they use HTTP, they fit into web services without new infrastructure. They need care, though. Network issues can cause missed notifications, so webhooks need proper retry mechanisms. The receiver should authenticate each incoming POST against spoofing and check its timestamp against replay. Options include an HMAC signature in a header, a shared secret, mutual TLS, or a sender IP list that is not sufficient alone. And because a sender lets users set an arbitrary destination URL, OWASP names webhooks a common vector for server-side request forgery. The mitigation is to re-check the resolved IP before each delivery, not only at registration.

sysd-msg-116.title: WebSocket API: opening and using a socket from a browser
sysd-msg-116.text: A browser opens a WebSocket with one constructor, new WebSocket(url [, protocols]), which starts the opening handshake. The URL scheme must be ws, wss, http or https, with no fragment. The send(data) call takes a string, Blob, ArrayBuffer or ArrayBufferView, and if the buffer is full the connection is closed and an error event fires. The API raises open, message, close and error events, and the close event reports a code, a reason and whether the closing handshake completed. The readyState is CONNECTING (0), OPEN (1), CLOSING (2) or CLOSED (3).

sysd-msg-104.title: HTTP streaming: a response that never ends
sysd-msg-104.text: The simplest way for a server to keep talking is never to finish the response. HTTP server push, also called HTTP streaming, sends unsolicited asynchronous data from a web server to a web browser. The server does not close the connection after serving the response, so an event can go out at once instead of waiting for the client's next request. It can use chunked transfer encoding or the multipart/x-mixed-replace content type from 1995. Browsers treat it as a document that changes with each push. Pushlets send snippets of JavaScript, but the server cannot control browser timeouts, and a timeout forces a page refresh.

sysd-msg-103.title: Server-sent events: a one-way stream over plain HTTP
sysd-msg-103.text: With server-sent events, or SSE, the client makes one request and the connection stays open. The server then sends events whenever new data is available. SSE is a server push technology in which a client receives automatic updates over an HTTP connection. The client requests a URL through the JavaScript EventSource API to receive an event stream, whose media type is text/event-stream. The mechanism was first specified in 2004, and the W3C published it as a recommendation on February 3, 2015. SSE is simple to implement for both client and server, supported by most browsers and causes no trouble with firewalls. Its limits are that it is unidirectional, so the client can only receive once its request is sent. The number of open connections is capped, and binary data is not supported. When sending high-frequency data, the server must manage backpressure to avoid saturating clients, with client-side buffering, adaptive limits on the event rate, or event batching. Real-time messaging and live location tracking can use either WebSockets or SSE.

sysd-msg-149.title: Presence information: who is free, busy or away
sysd-msg-149.text: The small icon beside a contact that says free for chat, busy, away or do not disturb is presence information. It is a status indicator that conveys the ability and willingness of a potential communication partner to communicate. A client publishes a presence state to a presence service, which stores it as the user's availability record, the presentity, and distributes it to interested users, called watchers. Presence from several devices can be aggregated and inferred from observation, such as marking a user Away when the keyboard is idle. Because presence is highly sensitive, a presentity may limit what each watcher sees, for example by blocking selected watchers.

sysd-msg-148.title: XMPP: federated chat protocol with presence
sysd-msg-148.text: Anyone can run an XMPP server, and there is no central master. XMPP is an open, XML-based communication protocol for real-time chat, presence information and contact list maintenance, with near-real-time exchange of structured data. The network is federated like email, and users on any server interoperate through a Jabber ID. It looks like an email address, username@domain, and an optional /resource suffix names one of the user's clients. A client sends a message to its own server, which delivers it instantly if the recipient is online and otherwise holds it. For a user on another server, it connects to that server. Clients connect over a TLS-encrypted TCP stream on port 5222, and servers talk to each other on port 5269. The native transport is long-lived TCP, with BOSH over HTTP for web clients and firewalled users, and XMPP can also use WebSockets. Extensions called XEPs add features such as multi-user chat and OMEMO encryption, which the server operator cannot decrypt. XML is text, so XMPP has higher network overhead than binary protocols, and large files are best sent out-of-band.

sysd-msg-150.title: Push message delivery controls: TTL, urgency and topic
sysd-msg-150.text: A web push message can be told how long to live, how urgent it is and which older message it replaces. The TTL header, in seconds, says how long the push service keeps the message for an intermittently connected device. After that the service must not deliver it. With a zero TTL the message goes out at once if the user agent is available and otherwise expires. The Urgency header, from very-low to high, helps battery-powered devices stay dormant. A Topic header of up to 32 characters makes a message replace any outstanding one with the same topic, so an offline device receives no outdated messages.

sysd-msg-119.title: Reconnecting a WebSocket with backoff
sysd-msg-119.text: After an abnormal closure, a client that reconnects at once can do harm. The closure may be transient, so reconnecting can work. If it is nontransient, clients that all reconnect immediately and persistently amount to a denial-of-service attack that can keep the service from recovering. So clients should back off. The first attempt should be delayed by a random time, and a value chosen randomly between 0 and 5 seconds is a reasonable initial delay. If it fails, later attempts should wait increasingly longer, as in {{ref:sysd-reliab-080}}. Terminated WebSocket connections are not automatically recovered, so the client has to do this itself.

sysd-msg-121.title: WebSocket URIs: ws and wss
sysd-msg-121.text: WebSocket defines two URI schemes: ws for unencrypted connections and wss for connections protected by TLS. A wss URI is called secure, and its traffic gets TLS's usual confidentiality, integrity and checking of who the endpoint is. The port is optional, with a default of 80 for ws and 443 for wss. The handshake requests a resource name, the path plus any query, or "/" when the path is empty. That lets one host and port serve several services. Fragment identifiers are meaningless in WebSocket URIs and must not be used.

sysd-msg-114.title: WebSocket security: origin checks, TLS and validation
sysd-msg-114.text: WebSocket requests are not restricted by the same-origin policy that limits regular cross-domain HTTP requests. So security rests on the browser's Origin header, TLS and whatever client check the server chooses. The Origin header tells the server which script origin made the request. A server meant only for certain sites should verify the origin and answer an unacceptable one with HTTP 403 Forbidden. Without that check, cross-site WebSocket hijacking, similar to {{ref:sysd-reliab-129}}, is possible when the connection is authenticated with cookies or HTTP credentials. The check stops trusted browsers running malicious JavaScript from faking a handshake, but not non-browser clients, which can send any Origin. The protocol prescribes no way to check a client. The options, such as cookies or tokens, are the subject of {{ref:sysd-reliab-015}}, and tokens are better when sensitive data is sent. Confidentiality and integrity come from TLS, through wss URIs. Both sides must validate incoming data, and implementations should cap frame and message sizes, since one huge frame or a long stream of small fragments can exhaust memory.

sysd-msg-118.title: WebSocket extensions: optional features negotiated up front
sysd-msg-118.text: A WebSocket can gain abilities such as compression, but only if both sides agree during the opening handshake. The base specification defines no extension. The client offers extensions in Sec-WebSocket-Extensions, in order of preference. The server accepts some or all by listing them in its response, and never lists one the client did not request. Order matters: operations are applied in the server's order, so "foo, bar" makes bar(foo(data)). Extensions can use the three reserved RSV bits and the extension data field. One example, permessage-deflate, compresses data messages with DEFLATE and sets RSV1 on the first frame.

sysd-msg-111.title: WebSocket masking: stopping scripts from forging HTTP on the wire
sysd-msg-111.text: In an experiment, attackers poisoned caching proxies by sending data on an upgraded connection that looked like an HTTP GET. Masking is the defense. A client XORs every frame it sends to the server with a random 32-bit key, so a script cannot control how its data looks on the wire. It does so whether or not TLS is used, with a fresh key for every frame. Each payload byte is XORed with the key byte at index i modulo 4, so the same algorithm masks and unmasks. A server must not mask its frames, and it must close the connection on receiving an unmasked one.

sysd-msg-112.title: WebSocket ping and pong: checking the other end is alive
sysd-msg-112.text: Ping and Pong are WebSocket control frames used as keepalive and heartbeat, to check that the other endpoint is still responsive. Either side may send a Ping at any time while the connection is open. It can serve as a keepalive, a latency measurement or a check on the remote endpoint. An endpoint that receives a Ping must answer with a Pong as soon as practical, carrying the same application data, unless it already received a Close frame. A Pong may also be sent unsolicited as a one-way heartbeat. No response is expected, and a Pong with no prior Ping is ignored.

sysd-msg-117.title: WebSocket subprotocols: agreeing what the messages mean
sysd-msg-117.text: WebSocket carries messages, and a subprotocol says what they mean. It is an application-level protocol layered over WebSocket messages, which client and server agree on in the opening handshake. The client lists the subprotocols it accepts in Sec-WebSocket-Protocol. The server selects one of those values and echoes it, and must not reply with a value the client did not offer. Names should be registered and should contain the ASCII domain name of the originator to avoid collisions, such as "chat.example.com". A backward-incompatible change is versioned by renaming the subprotocol, for example to "v2.bookings.example.net", which clients treat as completely separate. A backward-compatible change reuses the same string.

sysd-msg-120.title: WebSocket version negotiation
sysd-msg-120.text: What happens when a client asks for a WebSocket version the server does not speak? The refusal doubles as an offer. A client states the version it prefers in Sec-WebSocket-Version, which need not be the latest it supports. If the server supports it and the handshake is otherwise valid, the server accepts. If not, the server must answer with Sec-WebSocket-Version header fields listing every version it is willing to use. An HTTP error such as 426 Upgrade Required can carry them. A client that supports one of the advertised versions can then repeat the handshake with that version value.

sysd-msg-146.title: Comet: the workaround WebSocket made obsolete
sysd-msg-146.text: The standardization of WebSocket and server-sent events, widely supported since 2020, has made Comet obsolete. Comet was a web application model in which a long-held HTTPS request lets a web server push data to a browser without the browser explicitly requesting it. The name covers several techniques that give the browser two-way sustained interaction with the server. Implementations fall into streaming, with one persistent connection for all events, and long polling, where each response ends the request and the browser opens a new one. No streaming transport works in every browser, so many applications used long polling, which works wherever XHR does.

sysd-msg-147.title: The C10k problem: ten thousand connections at once
sysd-msg-147.text: Serving ten thousand clients at once used to be a hard problem, and it is now solved. By the early 2010s a commodity server held millions of connections, for example WhatsApp over 2 million with Erlang and MigratoryData 10-12 million with Java. The C10k problem was optimizing networking stacks for ten thousand concurrent clients. Many concurrent connections are not the same as many requests per second. The latter needs high throughput, the former efficient scheduling of connections to sockets or other stateful endpoints. Nginx was originally developed to solve C10k and handles more than 10,000 simultaneous connections with a low memory footprint.

sysd-msg-151.title: Running a push service: connections, storage and security
sysd-msg-151.text: A push service has to hold a very large number of open TCP connections, and storing messages for their TTL can take a significant amount of storage. Reliable delivery with receipts avoids retransmissions and polling. Without it, a device must acknowledge directly to the application server at extra power cost. The protocol must use HTTP over TLS, but TLS does not hide content from the push service. Applications must add end-to-end confidentiality, integrity and a way to check who sent a message. Push URIs should be hard to guess, and a push service should limit the message rate per user agent, for example by answering 429 with Retry-After.

openers.real-time-communication: A client that wants fresh information has several options. Polling means repeatedly checking a service for its status, and long polling has the server hold the request open until new information is available or a timeout is reached. Push technology turns the exchange around, so the server rather than the client starts it, as in push notifications and in web push, which delivers real-time events such as incoming calls or messages over HTTP/2. Or the browser and server can cooperate over WebSocket, a bidirectional channel over a single TCP connection that begins with an HTTP Upgrade request and a 101 response, then exchanges frames and closes with its own handshake. A notification system adds the machinery to validate, schedule and deliver messages through channels such as in-app messages, email, SMS and social media pushes.

reviews.real-time-communication: Polling has the client keep asking, long polling holds each request open, and push technology lets the server start the exchange, whether through server-sent events, webhooks or push notifications. WebSocket gives the strongest form of this, a persistent channel open in both directions, and its handshakes, frames, masking, ping and pong, subprotocols and extensions are small rules that keep it working and safe. Around it sit practical concerns: proxies and load balancers that must hold connections open, reconnecting with backoff, origin checks and TLS, and a notification architecture that routes messages through queues. Presence and XMPP show the same machinery serving chat. The C10k problem explains why holding so many connections was once hard, and it is now solved.
